reader.title: Lynching of William Henry Smith
bases: Masked men took an accused prisoner from the sheriff at the Wytheville depot and hanged and shot him (A1, A3, A7).

A 'body of masked men' or mob seized the man from the sheriff's custody, hanged him and riddled his body with bullets (A1, A3, A7); they acted on the accusation that he had assaulted a white woman in Pulaski county (A1, A9).

The Richmond Dispatch's Wytheville correspondent (A1), the Lynchburg Virginian special (A7, A6), the Baltimore/Wytheville wire (A3, A9) and the Roanoke Times (A14) agree on the seizure from the sheriff, the hanging and the shooting.

summary.text: The lynching of William Henry Smith was the hanging and shooting of a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman in Pulaski County, Virginia, by masked men who took him from the sheriff of Wythe County at the Wytheville depot around midnight in July 1888.
Smith, whom other reports called Henry Smith or William Jones, was hanged near the depot and his body riddled with bullets.
A wire from Wytheville carried the story nationally, several papers under headlines that endorsed the killing.

According to a New River special to the Lynchburg Virginian, reprinted in the Shenandoah Herald, a "strange negro man" asked Mrs. Midkiff for food, followed her into her house and assaulted her, then fled by train and was arrested on the line.
That night a mob of twenty-five took him from Deputy Sheriff Morgan, beat him with sticks after the woman could not positively identify him, and returned him to the deputy.
A later dispatch in the same paper repeated a report that he had been hanged and sunk in New River.
The Richmond Dispatch, which named the woman Mrs. Metcalfe, explained that Pulaski officers had instead evaded the lynchers by travelling all night in a buggy and lodged him in the Wytheville jail.
Late on the afternoon before the lynching, County Judge Holbrook learned that a mob was forming to storm the jail and ordered Sheriff Harkrader to take the prisoner secretly to Lynchburg.
Deputies kept him at an "unfrequented spot" outside town until the 11 o'clock train and put him aboard.

Some of the mob had come on that train from Rural Retreat, and they noosed him and dragged him from the car while the officers, in the Dispatch's words, "were powerless and made no further resistance."
He was hanged to a tree on Boyd's Hill, 200 yards from the depot by the Dispatch's account and 400 by the wire's, and his body was riddled with bullets.
Citizens found the body about an hour later.
The wire said the men were from Pulaski County, while the Lynchburg special called them unknown but "supposed to be from Pulaski."
The wire also stated that Smith was given time to pray and confessed; the Dispatch reported the confession only as a rumor the officers doubted.
No report of an inquest or an arrest of the Wytheville lynchers appears in the coverage, and the Dispatch called the town "perfectly quiet."
The Roanoke Times, reprinted in the Richmond Daily Times, named the dead man William Jones, whose wife received a letter from the Wythe sheriff about his death.
It reported that she thought he had met "his just deserts" and that acquaintances "white and colored" considered his punishment just, though the summary process was "not, of course, wholly approved."
The core report moved as a Wytheville special by way of Baltimore and ran from July 12 to 18 in papers from Delaware and Ohio to Texas, Georgia and Missouri.

Its headlines ranged from the San Antonio Daily Light's "A Well Deserved Fate" and the Springfield Daily Republic's "A Colored Demon Lynched" to the Delaware Daily Republican's "Hung Without Trial," and the Atlanta Constitution headlined the prayer.
Virginia papers such as the Alexandria Gazette used the Lynchburg version, which stated flatly that Smith "committed the outrage."

The Richmond Dispatch called him "THE PULASKI PIEND [FIEND]" whose "dastardly deed" brought "the awful penalty," and the Shenandoah Herald said the people, "thinking justice was too tardy," took the matter into their own hands.

The New York Sun, in a Sunday column on "Some Religious Occurrences," set the lynching beside a Pennsylvania crowd that prayed instead of hanging a tramp, remarking that the lynchers "were, of course, anxious that he should go straight to hell."
Besides the variant names, the woman was Mrs. Metcalfe "in a delicate condition" in the Dispatch but Mrs. Midkiff, an "aged lady," in the Lynchburg Virginian's report.
Dispatches datelined July 11 placed the lynching "last night," and the Alexandria Gazette said Tuesday night, while later wire versions, the Sun and the Roanoke Times said Wednesday night.
The two earliest accounts, both written the morning after, point to about midnight on July 10-11.

accounts.label: Richmond Dispatch Wytheville correspondent
accounts.gist: The judge ordered the prisoner moved; mob members who had come on the train from Rural Retreat dragged him from the car, hanged him on Boyd's Hill and riddled the body; a confession was rumored but doubted by officers.

accounts.label: Wytheville/Baltimore wire
accounts.gist: Masked men from Pulaski county took William Smith from Sheriff Harkrader at midnight, hanged him in a grove 400 yards away, shot the body, and gave him time to pray, when he confessed.

accounts.label: Lynchburg Virginian special
accounts.gist: Henry Smith was taken from the cars while being moved to Lynchburg, hanged and shot by unknown parties supposed to be from Pulaski.

accounts.label: New River and Radford reports
accounts.gist: A tramp who had asked for food assaulted Mrs. Midkiff, was arrested on the railroad, taken by a mob of 25 that beat him and returned him, and later rumored hanged and sunk in New River.

accounts.label: Roanoke Times
accounts.gist: The dead man was William Jones of Roanoke, whose wife and acquaintances thought his punishment just.

framing.detail: The San Antonio Daily Light headed the wire 'A Well Deserved Fate'; the Springfield Daily Republic used 'A Colored Demon Lynched' and 'A Rapist Lynched'.
The Richmond Dispatch called him 'THE PULASKI PIEND' who paid 'the awful penalty' while terming the lynchers a mob and noting the officers doubted the confession.
The Shenandoah Herald said the people, 'thinking justice was too tardy,' took the matter into their own hands; the Roanoke Times reported a local verdict of just punishment.
The Delaware Daily Republican ran the wire as 'Hung Without Trial'; the Atlanta Constitution and New Haven Morning Journal headlined the prayer.
The New York Sun contrasted the lynchers with a Pennsylvania crowd that prayed instead of hanging a tramp and called that course 'legal' and 'truly plous'.

conflicts.note: All describe the same man hanged at Wytheville; the Roanoke Times's name comes from the man's wife and acquaintances in Roanoke.
